I used to go to the plant every single day.
On Mondays I would drive the eighty kilometres before six.
I am used to getting up at five now.
It took a year to get used to not being in the building.
Ten years in the chair. What do you do now that you did not do at the start?
Almost the opposite of everything. I used to be in one of the plants every single day. I was extremely hands-on, and for about three years that was the right answer.
And then it stopped being the right answer.
Then we opened the second plant. That was the turning point. On Mondays I would drive eighty kilometres before six, and I was still the slowest part of every decision.
What did stepping back actually cost you?
A year of things being done worse than I would have done them. Doing it myself had been a crutch — it was faster and it taught nobody anything.
And now? Be honest with me. What have you not changed?
Pricing. It is my blind spot and I know it, which does not seem to help. I am used to being out of the building, but I am not used to somebody else setting a price.
I used to be in one of the plants every single day.
On Mondays I would drive out before six, and I was proud of it.
I am used to being out of the building now.
It took a year to get used to not doing it myself.
Doing it myself was a crutch. It was faster and it taught nobody anything.

I took over from my father in two thousand and twelve and I ran the company the way I had watched him run it, which is what everybody does and almost nobody admits. I used to sign every order over a certain value, and the value had been set in the nineteen nineties and never moved, so by the time I took over I was signing three hundred pieces of paper a month for amounts that did not matter. On Mondays I would come in at half past five to get through them before anybody arrived, and I was proud of that. It took a new finance manager about a fortnight to ask me what the number was for and why it had never changed. I did not have an answer. The honest version is that I was not defending a policy, I was repeating one, and repeating something is not the same as deciding it. I am used to not signing them now, and the odd thing is that I cannot remember the transition at all.

The pattern I see most often is not somebody refusing to change. It is somebody who changed the company and forgot to change themselves at the same time. The behaviour that got them here is usually a real strength, and that is exactly the problem, because you do not question the thing that worked. So the founder who used to know every customer by name is still trying to know every customer by name at four hundred accounts, and he is not being stubborn, he is being consistent with a version of the business that no longer exists. What I ask people to do is a small exercise, and almost everybody finds it uncomfortable. List five things you do every week. Then, for each one, say when you started doing it and what problem it solved at the time. About half of them turn out to be solving a problem the company had in a year you can name, and does not have now. Nobody needs persuading after that. The list does the work.

Business schools have looked at this for decades and the finding that survives is a slightly deflating one. Companies whose founder steps back from daily operations do not, on average, perform better in the following two years. They perform slightly worse, and then the line crosses somewhere in year three. Which means that everybody who does this correctly spends about two years being told, by their own numbers, that they were wrong. Interviews with owners who came out the other side turn up the same detail again and again. The hard part was never the decision. It was the middle period, when the founder could still do every job faster than the person now doing it, and the temptation to take one back was constant. The ones who did take a task back describe it in almost identical language: they say they only meant to help for a week. And the researchers make the same dry observation each time, which is that a week is exactly how long it takes for everybody to understand that the job is still yours.
